title: Justice

overview.intro: Justice is the standard by which institutions and decisions are judged, and the two theories that dominate contemporary debate — John Rawls’s justice as fairness and Amartya Sen’s capability approach — disagree about what the standard is. This unit examines the meaning of justice and its classical formulation in Aristotle, then the features of Rawls’s principles and the original position, and Sen’s critique and alternative, before assessing what each offers political practice.

facts.label: Classical formula
facts.value: Aristotle: justice is giving to each what is his due, with distributive justice allocating shares according to a relevant standard.

facts.label: Rawls
facts.value: Justice as fairness: two principles chosen behind a veil of ignorance — equal basic liberties, and inequality permitted only if it benefits the least advantaged.

facts.label: Sen
facts.value: Justice is not about ideal institutions but about what people are actually able to do and be; compare real freedoms, not rules or resources.

facts.label: Central dispute
facts.value: Whether justice is best defined by the principles governing a just basic structure or by the capabilities people achieve.

learningOutcomes: Define justice and distinguish its distributive and retributive aspects.
Explain the features of Rawls’s two principles and the original position.
Explain Sen’s capability approach and his critique of transcendental institutionalism.
Compare Rawls and Sen on the object of justice.
Assess which theory better guides actual political decisions.

blocks.text: Justice is the quality of giving to each person what is due to them, and it divides into several working branches. Distributive justice governs the allocation of benefits and burdens among members of a community; retributive justice governs the punishment of wrongdoing in proportion to fault; corrective justice restores the position of a person wronged by another; and procedural justice concerns the fairness of the process itself, which is why a rule applied by an interested judge fails justice even if its content is sound. The branches share one structure — a relevant standard determines what is due — and differ only in what is being allocated and by what criterion.

Aristotle’s formulation remains the starting point: justice is equality for equals, and the unequal are to receive shares unequal in proportion to their worth. He distinguished distribution according to merit from rectification according to loss, and he insisted that the standard must be relevant — allocation by lot is just where offices are equal, distribution by contribution where rewards are at stake. Modern theories keep the form while arguing about the standard: whether what is due is founded on desert, need, equality or the choices free persons would make behind fair conditions.

blocks.text: Rawls asks what principles would be chosen for the basic structure of society by persons concerned to further their own interests but situated so that they cannot know their own position — their class, talents, conception of the good, or the generation to which they belong. Behind this veil of ignorance, in the original position, no one can tailor principles to advantage, so the choice is fair. Rawls argues that rational parties would choose two principles in lexical order: first, each person has an equal right to the most extensive basic liberties compatible with the same liberty for all; second, social and economic inequalities are to be arranged so that they are both attached to offices open to all under conditions of fair equality of opportunity and to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society.

Two features of the second principle distinguish Rawls from every earlier theory. The difference principle permits inequality, but only as an incentive that improves the position of the worst-off group — a factory owner may earn more only where the arrangement that produces the greater return also raises the floor for the least advantaged. And the lexical order means basic liberty cannot be traded away for economic gain: a society may not restrict speech in order to increase output, because the first principle has priority. Rawls also supplies the intuition that fairness concerns the terms of cooperation rather than the outcome of competition, which is why he treats the natural distribution of talent as neither just nor unjust — it is a natural fact — while holding that the scheme that distributes its rewards is entirely a matter of choice.

learn.title: Sen: justice and the capability approach

blocks.text: Sen accepts much of Rawls’s moral territory but rejects the route. His objection is to what he calls transcendental institutionalism: theories that ask what a perfectly just institution would look like, and then judge the world by its distance from that ideal. The objection is practical — a perfect standard yields little guidance when several arrangements are imperfect and one must be chosen — and it is also a matter of focus, since institutions are means and the proper object of attention is what people are actually able to do and be. Justice, on this view, is realised in the real freedoms people enjoy rather than declared by the rules under which they live.

Sen’s alternative evaluates capabilities — the substantive freedoms to be nourished, to be educated, to participate, to live without shame — and functionings, the states a person actually achieves. Two people with identical rights and income may have very different capabilities if illness, disability or social prejudice blocks one of them, which is why resources are an unreliable measure. Sen insists on comparative judgement rather than perfect diagnosis: we can recognise that one arrangement gives people more real freedom than another without claiming to know what the best would be, and public reasoning about what counts as a capability is itself part of the just process. He also insists that no single criterion — utility, resources or rights — can settle all distributive questions, a position he calls pluralism of criteria.

learn.title: Assessment: what each theory offers political practice

blocks.text: Rawls’s strengths are precision and priority. His principles can be applied to a constitution and a basic economic scheme, the lexical order protects rights from being bargained away, and the difference principle supplies a demanding test that most actual inequalities fail. The criticisms are well known: Nozick objected that end-state principles ignore how holdings were acquired and disturb liberty in the process; communitarians argued that the original position strips persons of the attachments that give choices meaning; and the difference principle has been attacked both from the right as discouraging enterprise and from the left as still permitting very large inequalities so long as the floor rises.

Sen’s strengths are flexibility and focus on the person: he explains why identical rules produce unequal lives, he accommodates plural values, and his method fits the real decision, which is usually a choice among imperfect options. The criticisms are that capabilities require a list, and who decides the list reintroduces the kind of judgement Sen wished to avoid; that his comparative method offers no principle of distribution at all, so it can rank arrangements without telling us what each person is due; and that institutions, however imperfect, are what actually secure freedoms over time, which pulls the argument back toward Rawls. The most useful conclusion for an exam is that the two are complementary in practice: Rawls supplies the principles that define a fair basic structure, and Sen supplies the test — what people can actually do and be — by which those principles are checked against reality, so that a society formally compliant with the difference principle is still judged on the capabilities its members achieve.

questions.answer: The first principle may not be sacrificed for economic gain

questions.explanation: The relevant standard determines what is due, whether merit, need, or loss to be rectified.

questions.explanation: Capabilities, not resources, capture what a person is genuinely able to do and be.

questions.prompt: State Rawls’s two principles of justice in their order of priority.
questions.answer: The first principle is that each person has an equal right to the most extensive scheme of equal basic liberties compatible with the same scheme of liberty for all. The second principle states that social and economic inequalities are to be arranged so that they are both attached to positions and offices open to all under conditions of fair equality of opportunity, and to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society. The order matters: the principles are lexically ordered, so the first may never be traded for economic gain, and within the second, fair equality of opportunity takes priority over the difference principle.
questions.explanation: Both principles must be stated with the lexical order and the two clauses of the second principle.

questions.prompt: Explain two features of the capability approach as an account of justice.
questions.answer: The first feature is its object: justice is assessed by capabilities — the substantive freedoms a person has to achieve states they have reason to value, such as being nourished, educated, participating in community life and living without shame — rather than by the resources they hold or the rules under which they live. Two people with identical rights and income can have very different capabilities where illness, disability or prejudice blocks one of them, which is why resources are an unreliable measure. The second feature is its method: Sen rejects transcendental institutionalism, which seeks the perfectly just institution, and insists instead on comparative judgement — ranking feasible arrangements by the real freedoms they secure, using public reasoning about what counts as a capability. A third accepted feature is pluralism: no single criterion such as utility, resources or rights can settle every distributive question, so several standards are weighed together.
questions.explanation: Two features must be given as features — object and method — with the reason each matters.

questions.prompt: Compare Rawls and Sen as accounts of justice, and state what each offers political practice.
questions.answer: The two theories agree that justice concerns the fairness of the terms on which people live together and disagree about where that fairness is located and how it is to be found. Rawls locates it in principles: persons in the original position, ignorant of their class, talents and conception of the good, would choose equal basic liberties first, fair equality of opportunity second and the requirement that inequality benefit the least advantaged third, with the principles lexically ordered so that no economic gain can purchase a reduction in basic liberty. His method is therefore transcendental in the useful sense — establish what a just basic structure requires, then judge institutions against it — and his practical offerings are precision, priority for rights, and a demanding test that most existing inequalities fail. Sen accepts the moral destination but rejects the route. He objects that a theory of perfect institutions yields little guidance when every real choice is between imperfect alternatives, and he shifts the object from institutions to capabilities, the real freedoms people have to function. His method is comparative: rank the arrangements actually available by the capabilities they secure for their members, using public reasoning, and accept that several criteria — resources, rights, utility — must be weighed rather than reduced to one. The differences have consequences. Rawls can tell you whether a tax scheme satisfies the difference principle; Sen can tell you that the scheme leaves a disabled person with no real freedom to use the benefits, which Rawls’s primary-goods measure would miss. Conversely Sen can rank two societies but cannot say what each individual is due, which is exactly what Rawls supplies. The balanced conclusion is that they operate at different stages: Rawls defines the fair structure, Sen tests whether people actually achieve freedom within it, and a political practice that uses both is better than either alone.
questions.explanation: Full marks need both theories with their object and method, at least one concrete application of each, and a conclusion about how they relate rather than a winner.

questions.prompt: Can a society be formally compliant with the difference principle and still be unjust? Discuss using the capability approach.
questions.answer: The case that formal compliance can coexist with injustice is precisely Sen’s argument, and it can be made concretely. Suppose a society secures equal basic liberties, opens offices to competitive examination and arranges its economy so that the returns to talent raise the floor of the worst-off group: on Rawls’s test as literally stated, it satisfies both principles. Yet suppose further that a quarter of the population, because of disability, caste, gendered exclusion from public space or regional deprivation, cannot convert those formal entitlements into any real freedom — the examination is passed but the interview excludes, the benefit is paid but the clinic is unreachable. Equal primary goods have been distributed while the capabilities of the worst-off within the worst-off group remain unachieved, which shows that a measure of advantage in resources and rights is not a reliable guide to what people are able to do and be. The response from the Rawlsian has three parts. First, Rawls is not purely formal: fair equality of opportunity requires active measures to correct precisely those disadvantages, and a society that ignored caste or disability would fail clause (a) of the second principle. Second, the difference principle is sensitive to the position of the least advantaged group, and if their real condition is unimproved then the arrangement does not satisfy it, so the failure is one of application rather than of theory. Third, institutions are what secure freedoms durably, and Sen’s comparative method gives no principle of distribution, so abandoning Rawls’s structure risks losing the priority of rights that protects the very people capability measures are designed to see. The strongest conclusion combines the two: the Rawlsian test must be applied with Sen’s evidence, since what counts as benefit to the least advantaged cannot be measured in holdings alone, while the capability assessment needs the lexical priority and institutional backbone that Rawls supplies. On that reading formal compliance is necessary but not sufficient — the question is never what people hold but what they are enabled to do — and a strong essay demonstrates this with a single worked case in which the two measures diverge.
questions.explanation: Full marks require a concrete case of divergence, the capability argument stated precisely, the strongest Rawlsian reply, and a synthesis rather than a verdict for one side.
